phase1.intro:
You've spent four units building the inside of a workshop nobody's ever seen. Unit 5 builds the storefront.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: What are Stage, Scene, and Scene Graph?
dialogue: Every JavaFX app has three pieces mapping onto the storefront: the [[term:Stage]] is the building itself — one per app, created before your code even runs. The [[term:Scene]] is whatever's arranged in the window right now. A [[term:Scene Graph]] is the arrangement itself: a tree of nodes, root holding children holding their own children.

stickyNote.flavor: 🏢 the building, the display, and the arrangement tree
stickyNote.definition: Stage = the window itself. Scene = what's currently displayed. Scene Graph = the tree structure of nodes (root → children → grandchildren).

topics.buttonText: How does a JavaFX app actually start?
dialogue: To open the shop, you extend [[term:Application]] and override `start(Stage primaryStage)`. Build your Scene, call `primaryStage.setScene(scene)`, then `primaryStage.show()`. [[warn:You never call start() yourself]] — `main()` calls `launch(args)`, which constructs the Stage and calls start() for you.

stickyNote.flavor: 🚪 launch() builds the Stage and calls start() for you
stickyNote.definition: extend Application, override start(Stage), call launch(args) from main(). You never call start() directly — launch() does that.

topics.buttonText: Why can't I update the UI from any thread I want?
dialogue: JavaFX runs its own dedicated thread — the [[term:JavaFX Application Thread]] — and [[warn:every UI update has to happen on it]]. Do background work off-thread and hand results back with `Platform.runLater()` — touching the window from another thread risks freezing or corrupting mid-render.

stickyNote.flavor: 🧵 all UI updates must happen on this one thread
stickyNote.definition: JavaFX UI updates must happen on its dedicated Application Thread. Background work should hand results back via Platform.runLater().

phase1.openingDialogue: Unit 5 builds the storefront — Stage, Scene, and the JavaFX Application Thread that all UI updates must run on. 🏢

phase2.explanation:
No broken code this time — this lesson is the floor plan, not a build. But two myths are worth clearing up before we start nailing shelves together.

"JavaFX is dead, Swing is the only real option" — [[warn:not true]]. JavaFX is still actively maintained by the OpenJFX project, and it's the recommended toolkit for new Java desktop UIs. It just isn't bundled inside the JDK anymore as of Java 11 — you add it as a separate dependency, the same way you'd add any library.

"JavaFX can only make simple toy windows" — also not true. [[key:JavaFX handles charts, embedded web views, media playback, 3D graphics, and full animation timelines]] — everything from this lesson's plain Label window to a genuinely polished, professional desktop app is the same toolkit, just more of it.

phase3.openingDialogue: JavaFX — modern GUI for modern apps! 🎨

mcq.question:
Which statement about JavaFX is TRUE?

A) JavaFX doesn't support CSS styling
B) All UI updates must happen on the JavaFX Application Thread
C) JavaFX applications don't use a main() method
D) JavaFX is older than Swing

Select the CORRECT statement.

phase5.trivia: Stage and Scene aren't Java-chan's naming choice — [[fun:JavaFX borrows its vocabulary straight from the theater]]. A Stage is the physical structure, a Scene is what's currently set up on it, and you can even swap Scenes on the same Stage the way a play changes sets without tearing down the building. The storefront metaphor and the theater metaphor are really pointing at the same idea: a fixed venue, changeable contents.
